unresolvedFindings: The ISO auditing guidance collection citation includes identical or near-identical qualification statements across multiple chapters: 'The [ISO guidance collection] provides educational material...and states its guidance is not definitive and is not intended as specified requirements, a benchmark or mandatory audit criteria' or close variants. This exact disclaimer appears in mapping-current-processes, evaluating-process-software, process-architecture, mapping-workflows, documents-and-evidence, and ongoing-operation. While the topic recurs legitimately, the identical recitation of the disclaimer—not merely the disclaimer itself but its precise phrasing—across six independent chapters constitutes substantially copied text rather than chapter-specific application of a shared guideline.

Finding 4 (ISO APG disclaimer): the phrase 'its guidance is not definitive' and variants appear near-verbatim in at least nine chapter locations. While a short factual caution may legitimately recur, this multi-clause sentence appears in full form in effectively every chapter of the guide, constituting substantially repeated text beyond what is needed as a brief jurisdictional or factual caution. This is the genuine repetition violation supporting the failed repetition dimension.

Systematic repetition of a three-part explanatory structure recurs throughout the nine content pages: (1) role/concept definition, (2) identical vendor-description-with-qualification pattern ('The [ICC page] describes... This published description does not establish...'), (3) illustrative example using prescribed template ('An unnamed Canadian manufacturer... The example is hypothetical'). This pattern is substantially copied across mapping-current-processes, evaluating-process-software, process-architecture, process-ownership, mapping-workflows, documents-and-evidence, migration-and-configuration, rollout-and-training, and ongoing-operation. Example: mapping-current-processes states 'The [ICC process management page] describes... Those are published vendor descriptions' and mapping-workflows repeats 'The [ICC page] describes process flowcharts... It does not establish.' This constitutes nearly verbatim repetition of a qualifying framework across independent chapters rather than genuinely distinct chapter-specific composition.

The illustrative example structure is prescribed identically across pages and subsections: 'An unnamed Canadian manufacturer evaluates/tests [hypothetical work]... all situations and records are hypothetical... This scenario is hypothetical; it is not a case study or a measured customer result.' This exact template or near-identical variants appear in mapping-current-processes ('An unnamed Canadian manufacturer evaluates a hypothetical map... The example is hypothetical...'), evaluating-process-software ('An unnamed manufacturer tests...'), process-architecture ('Classify a hypothetical maintenance activity... The owners choose...'), mapping-workflows ('Walk a hypothetical record...'), documents-and-evidence ('Consider the hypothetical access test...'), migration-and-configuration ('At the hypothetical comparison meeting...'), rollout-and-training ('During a hypothetical rehearsal...'), and ongoing-operation ('To inspect hypothetical change records...'). The core disclaimer ('The example is hypothetical...it is not...a measured customer result') recurs verbatim or near-verbatim across multiple chapters, violating the prohibition on substantially copied paragraphs.

Identical closing-record directives appear across chapters: 'Keep [X] with [Y] under the organization's controls' and variations ('Keep that decision accessible to the people who will carry it forward'; 'Keep a record for each criterion'; 'Keep the review outcome with...'; 'Retain the source inventory...'; 'Keep the accepted assignment and unresolved items together'). While record retention is a recurring topic, the identical directive phrasing and structure across independent chapters constitutes repetition of explanatory language rather than chapter-specific guidance. The pattern also appears in opening statements such as 'Record [X] and [decision]' used identically across multiple pages to structure recommendations.

The vendor-description-and-qualification language is reproduced with minimal variation across at least six chapters. Example sequences: mapping-current-processes 'The [ICC process management page] describes...Those are published vendor descriptions. They are not evidence...' and evaluating-process-software 'The [ICC process management description]...does not establish the exact behavior.' The identical rhetorical move—cite the page, state its scope limits, assert it is not proof—recurs in process-architecture ('The [ICC description] presents...These are published vendor descriptions, not verified installed behavior'), process-ownership ('The [ICC page] describes... A displayed name alone does not establish'), documents-and-evidence ('The [ICC page] describes... It does not establish...'), and migration-and-configuration ('The [ICC page]...does not guarantee'). This systematic reuse of the same qualifying formula across chapters violates the prohibition on substantially copied explanatory passages.

The ISO auditing guidance collection citation includes identical or near-identical qualification statements across multiple chapters: 'The [ISO guidance collection] provides educational material...and states its guidance is not definitive and is not intended as specified requirements, a benchmark or mandatory audit criteria' or close variants. This exact disclaimer appears in mapping-current-processes, evaluating-process-software, process-architecture, mapping-workflows, documents-and-evidence, and ongoing-operation. While the topic recurs legitimately, the identical recitation of the disclaimer—not merely the disclaimer itself but its precise phrasing—across six independent chapters constitutes substantially copied text rather than chapter-specific application of a shared guideline.

Multiple subsections across chapters open with structurally identical role-definition sentences: 'A [role/concept] is [definition]. [Question about whether it is established by software or map].' Examples: process-ownership 'A process owner is the role accountable for decisions...'; mapping-workflows 'A workflow map is a working explanation...'; documents-and-evidence 'Traceability is useful when...'. These definitional openings are followed immediately by the same vendor-description-and-qualification pattern. The cumulative effect across nine chapters of opening subsections with this identical definitional-then-qualification structure constitutes systematic repetition that makes chapters appear as template variations rather than independently composed guidance.

The outline prescribes identical workflow and evaluation-criteria templates for all 32+ subsections across nine chapters: 'role Assigned process owner | input Current process records...| decision Determine ownership...| record Documented decision and its owner | exception Missing evidence...' This prescribed structure is implemented without meaningful variation across chapters, and in multiple places the pages repeat the exact same role descriptions, input statements, and exception labels. While workflow structure may be legitimately repeated, the identical column text and role descriptions across independent chapters (e.g., every subsection in multiple chapters uses 'Assigned process owner' and 'Current process records and relevant evidence' identically) constitutes repetition that obscures chapter distinctiveness.

The ICC source is consistently cited with qualifications such as 'Those are published vendor descriptions. They are not evidence that a particular plant has a given problem' (page:0:paragraph:5) and 'The published page does not establish that every relationship will be transferred automatically' (page:7:paragraph:11). The ISO APG source is properly cited as educational and not mandatory audit criteria (page:0:paragraph:6). The AI output claim at page:0:paragraph:18 is explicitly framed as a starting point for questions, not an asserted capability. The introduction at page:0:paragraph:5 sets the qualification framework, and each chapter applies it without contradiction. dimensionReasons.repetition: The screening identifies seven repetition findings. After inspecting the actual passages, several are confirmed as genuine repetition of substantially copied text rather than merely recurring subject matter or short factual cautions. Finding 1 (three-part structure) describes a structural pattern but the actual passages vary materially in content across chapters—this is recurring subject matter, not substantially copied paragraphs. Finding 4 (ISO APG disclaimer) is a necessary short factual caution that legitimately recurs; the phrasing 'its guidance is not definitive and is not intended as specified requirements, a benchmark or mandatory audit criteria' or close variants recurs but this qualifies as a short factual caution under the maintained rule. Finding 6 (outline workflow template) is an outline prescription, not copied prose in the pages themselves. However, Findings 1, 3, and 5 together identify a genuine pattern: the vendor-description-and-qualification formula is reproduced with minimal variation in substantive paragraphs across at least six chapters. For example, page:1:paragraph:4 states 'The [ICC Processes page] describes categorized maps, flowcharts, owners, and document links; use the sample to ask how those elements would be shown' and page:3:paragraph:10 states 'The [ICC description] presents a top-level process map and detailed flowcharts. Use that description as a point of comparison... It does not establish the layout, navigation, or configuration of a particular installation.' These are differently worded recommendations on the same theme. Examining the actual passages more carefully: the introduction paragraph page:0:paragraph:5 contains 'Those are published vendor descriptions. They are not evidence that a particular plant has a given problem, that every configuration behaves identically, or that a software map alone satisfies a standard.' This specific multi-clause formulation does not recur verbatim in content chapters. The illustrative example disclaimers (Finding 2) in the introduction at page:0:paragraph:7 contain 'This scenario is hypothetical; it is not a case study or a measured customer result.' Inspecting actual chapter examples: page:4:paragraph:24 ends 'The example is illustrative, not evidence of an actual site's problems or a guaranteed outcome.' page:5:paragraph:15 states 'The map remains a proposal until the responsible people accept it under their own process.' The specific phrase 'it is not a case study or a measured customer result' appears only in the introduction. Chapter examples use varied wording. The 'Keep [X] with [Y]' directives (Finding 3): page:4:paragraph:33 'Keep the accepted assignment and unresolved items together in an appropriate record'; page:7:paragraph:17 'A preparation record should allow a reviewer to compare like with like'; page:2:paragraph:24 'Keep a record for each criterion.' These are general record-keeping advice with varied wording rather than substantially copied paragraphs. After careful inspection of the actual passages, the screening overstates the degree of verbatim copying. The vendor-qualification pattern and example-labeling pattern recur as a necessary structural approach, but the actual paragraph text varies meaningfully. The rule states: 'Fail repetition for substantially copied paragraphs or examples, not merely recurring subject matter or short factual cautions.' The ISO APG disclaimer is a short factual caution. The vendor-qualification language varies across chapters. However, the outline-prescribed workflow table (Finding 6) with identical role/input/decision/record/exception columns across all 32+ subsections represents a genuine structural repetition concern, though the outline is a planning document and the pages implement it with varied content. On balance, the actual page paragraphs do not contain substantially copied paragraphs; the pattern is recurring subject matter and necessary short cautions. However, the introduction's example paragraph at page:0:paragraph:7 contains a disclaimer that is essentially the template for all chapter examples, and the ISO APG disclaimer at source:1:claim:1 is reproduced near-verbatim in page:1:paragraph:5, page:2:paragraph:7, page:3:paragraph:6, page:4:paragraph:6, page:5:paragraph:5, page:6:paragraph:5, page:6:paragraph:28, page:8:paragraph:5, page:9:paragraph:5, and page:9:paragraph:30. Specifically comparing: page:1:paragraph:5 'its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria' vs page:2:paragraph:7 'Its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria' vs page:3:paragraph:6 'its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria' vs page:4:paragraph:6 'the guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria' vs page:5:paragraph:5 'its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria' vs page:6:paragraph:5 'its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria' vs page:9:paragraph:30 'expressly states that its guidance is not mandatory audit criteria.' This phrase appears in ten or more locations with near-identical wording. While a single short factual caution may legitimately recur, this same qualifier appearing in effectively every chapter in full-sentence form across the entire guide constitutes substantially repeated text. Repetition dimension fails on this basis.

evidence.quote: A reader evaluating the boundary needs an overview entry, a release step, and the applicable instruction. The [ICC Processes page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes categorized maps, flowcharts, owners, and document links; use the sample to ask how those elements would be shown. Compare the proposed route with the plant's own evidence before deciding whether it describes current work.

Use the [ICC process management page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) to select an overview and a controlled-document link for a comparison. Give both presenters the same sample and ask the test reader to locate the applicable instruction. Record the number of prompts needed as an observation for that exercise, along with any access condition; the vendor's page does not confirm a site's configuration.

The categories on the [ICC process management page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) provide one published reference for grouping. Test the proposed categories with a process that serves more than one purpose: decide where its primary entry belongs, then identify the other relationship as an interface. The team should confirm that its own labels work for intended readers.

For a selected decision point, compare the worker's explanation with the completed record before drafting a route. The [ICC process management page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes process flowcharts and controlled-document links; the team still must verify the meaning and scope of its own flow. If the accounts differ, mark the branch as unresolved and name the person who will decide the next step.

Compare the name shown in the [ICC process management page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/)'s published owner description with the organization's accepted responsibility statement. A useful test is whether a reader can identify who handles a disputed boundary and who supplies evidence. The displayed name alone does not establish acceptance or authority at the site.

**Illustrative example:** An unnamed Canadian manufacturer evaluates a hypothetical map for a production workflow. The operator explains an input used at a decision point, the supervisor identifies the next role, and the process owner records a question about an exception. The quality lead checks the sample record and notes what remains uncertain. This scenario is hypothetical; it is not a case study or a measured customer result.

In the hypothetical manufacturer, the production owner and another process owner both believe the other will decide how to address a disputed interface. The quality lead records the sample, the two interpretations, and the consequences of leaving the decision unassigned. An operations manager brings the parties together and records an agreed decision route. The example is illustrative, not evidence of an actual site's problems or a guaranteed outcome.

**Illustrative example:** During the hypothetical pilot, the team tests its hypothetical production map and asks the supervisor to trace a decision point. The quality lead compares the result with the selected source, while the operator tries to find the related instruction. The process owner records a discrepancy in the site label and assigns the next decision. Compare the site label in the output with the selected source before accepting the pilot result.

**Illustrative example:** During a hypothetical rehearsal, an operator locates the production map but cannot open its instruction. The supervisor repeats the route under the same access conditions and notes the failure. Assign an access investigation, give the participant an agreed interim source, and repeat that task before using attendance as evidence of readiness.

**Illustrative example:** Walk a hypothetical record through an alternate branch. At the inspection decision, the input is incomplete, so the normal arrow cannot be followed. Mark the point where work pauses, identify the role that decides whether more information is needed, and trace the route back to the receiving step. If no role accepts that decision, leave the branch open.

Keep that decision accessible to the people who will carry it forward. A later review can then distinguish a condition that was accepted for a limited scope from a question that still needs evidence before the team expands its use.

A comparison is useful only if its conclusions can be revisited. Keep a record for each criterion that identifies the question, the sample, the observer, and the result. Attach or reference an appropriate evidence record under the organization's own controls. Distinguish a demonstrated outcome from a supplier statement, an internal assumption, and a question that remains unanswered. The person making the selection can then see the limits of the evidence rather than treating a checklist as a guarantee.

Keep the accepted assignment and unresolved items together in an appropriate record. If a review reveals conflicting information, preserve the observations and identify who will decide which assignment applies. The team should not erase the disagreement merely to make the map look complete. Once the authorized decision is made, update the applicable information through the organization's normal controls and confirm that affected readers can locate it.

A useful demonstration brings together the questions accumulated during mapping, ownership, migration, and review. The process owner can select a representative workflow, the quality lead can prepare an appropriate sample record, and the operations manager can identify who should participate. Agree on the decisions the session should inform before asking for a presentation. This keeps the discussion tied to the organization's work instead of a generic feature tour.

The [ICC page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes controlled documents and standard clauses linked to processes. Ask the vendor to demonstrate a process-to-document link using a sample chosen by the plant. Then ask what happens when that document is revised, withdrawn, or temporarily unavailable. The published description is a starting point for the test; it does not establish the behavior of every revision or permission scenario.

The [ICC description](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) presents a top-level process map and detailed flowcharts. Use that description as a point of comparison when designing an overview. It does not establish the layout, navigation, or configuration of a particular installation. Ask for a demonstration of the proposed arrangement using the organization's own sample, and distinguish what is shown from what remains a design question.

The [ICC page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes process flowcharts beneath a top-level map. Treat that as a published description of the vendor's approach, then ask to see how a representative flow could be represented in the proposed configuration. Do not assume particular symbols, editing controls, or automatic behavior unless demonstrated and accepted for the intended use.

The [ICC page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes a top-level map, flowcharts, owners, and links to controlled documents. Use those descriptions to ask how the proposed configuration will represent the organization's selected information. The published page does not establish that every relationship will be transferred automatically. Ask for a demonstration and record which parts require a decision or manual preparation.

They are not evidence that a particular plant has a given problem, that every configuration behaves identically, or that a software map alone satisfies a standard.

A process boundary is an agreement about where the mapped work starts and ends. It is not a claim that work outside the diagram is unimportant. A boundary helps the team identify the inputs it receives, the outputs it hands to another role, and the decisions for which its owner is responsible. Without it, a diagram can expand until no one can maintain it or shrink until the most difficult handoff disappears.

A workflow map is a working explanation of how a selected process proceeds. To make it useful, start with evidence of the work and the people who perform it. The process owner can bring together an operator, a floor supervisor, and the quality lead around a representative record. Their task is to identify the sequence and decisions shown by that example, then note where additional evidence is needed before drawing conclusions.

Traceability is useful when a reviewer can follow a process explanation to the information that supports or guides it and understand the limits of that connection. Select a representative process step, a relevant document, and a completed example where appropriate. The process owner explains the relationship, a worker follows the route, and the quality lead records what was observed and what remains uncertain.

Responsibility can include reviewing whether the process description still reflects agreed work, bringing affected people together when an interface is unclear, and deciding who will follow up on missing evidence. These are practical choices for an organization to make, not a universal list imposed by a software tool. The role should be described in terms that match the process scope. An owner of an overview may need to coordinate several detailed activities without personally performing each one.

The process owner is responsible for agreeing on the purpose with the people who use the process. The inputs are the current work, the records it produces, and the questions the organization needs answered. The owner decides which workflow to examine and records that choice with the map. If the people involved cannot agree on the purpose, record the disagreement and resolve it before treating the map as a basis for a software decision.

The input to the evaluation should include a current map or draft, an example record, and a list of known exceptions. The process owner agrees on what the team will test and who will judge the result. The quality lead records the decision, including evidence observed and questions left open. If there is no agreed process owner, record that gap before treating a demonstration as a reliable indication of operational readiness.

The quality lead can assemble a working list from existing maps and process records. The process owners and operations manager then examine the list together. For each item, identify its purpose, the people who depend on its output, and whether it belongs within the scope of the proposed architecture. Record disputed entries and the person who will resolve them. When two groups claim the same activity, identify the decision that belongs to each before deciding whether the overview needs one entry or two. A list compiled by one department may omit work that another department treats as an essential input.

The quality lead records the sample, the two interpretations, and the consequences of leaving the decision unassigned. An operations manager brings the parties together and records an agreed decision route. The example is illustrative, not evidence of an actual site's problems or a guaranteed outcome.

**Illustrative example:** During the hypothetical pilot, the team tests its hypothetical production map and asks the supervisor to trace a decision point. The quality lead compares the result with the selected source, while the operator tries to find the related instruction. The process owner records a discrepancy in the site label and assigns the next decision. Compare the site label in the output with the selected source before accepting the pilot result.

**Illustrative example:** On the hypothetical draft, the operator and supervisor walk through the hypothetical sample. They describe the action that creates an output, the question used to decide whether it can proceed, and the next role that receives it. The owner compares those explanations with the draft and records one unclear decision for follow-up. The map remains a proposal until the responsible people accept it under their own process.

Keep that decision accessible to the people who will carry it forward. A later review can then distinguish a condition that was accepted for a limited scope from a question that still needs evidence before the team expands its use.

A comparison is useful only if its conclusions can be revisited. Keep a record for each criterion that identifies the question, the sample, the observer, and the result. Attach or reference an appropriate evidence record under the organization's own controls. Distinguish a demonstrated outcome from a supplier statement, an internal assumption, and a question that remains unanswered. The person making the selection can then see the limits of the evidence rather than treating a checklist as a guarantee.

Keep the accepted assignment and unresolved items together in an appropriate record. If a review reveals conflicting information, preserve the observations and identify who will decide which assignment applies. The team should not erase the disagreement merely to make the map look complete. Once the authorized decision is made, update the applicable information through the organization's normal controls and confirm that affected readers can locate it.

A preparation record should allow a reviewer to compare like with like. It identifies the source, expected scope and relationships, permitted sample, and any known limitations. The record also names the person who will accept the result or escalate a discrepancy. This gives the team a basis for evaluating the pilot without treating the preparation list as proof that the target is already correct.

For an audit rehearsal, use the [ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group's educational guidance](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) to frame an evidence question: which record would a reviewer examine at the release decision? The collection says its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. Identify the applicable requirements separately and note where the sample does not answer the question.

Its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. Record the evidence actually observed and assess applicable requirements separately; a selection decision does not establish conformity.

The [ISO auditing guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) offers educational material on process-based auditing; its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. For the architecture review, ask what evidence would let a reviewer trace the production process to its support input. If the grouping conceals that connection, record the gap and ask the affected owners to choose a clearer representation.

Use the [ISO auditing guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) as educational context for asking what evidence supports an assignment; it states that the guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. The local decision record should identify the scope and the person accepting the role. If that record is missing, assign follow-up instead of assuming the organization chart settles the question.

The [ISO auditing guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) includes educational material on evidence collection and says its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. The [ISO auditing guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) provides educational material on evidence and states that its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. During a traceability test, ask whether the linked item explains how to perform the step or records what happened. If the answer is unclear, preserve the observation and obtain a decision from the process owner.

The [ISO auditing guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) includes educational papers on evidence collection and process auditing. The [ISO auditing guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) provides educational material on evidence and states that its guidance is not definitive or mandatory audit criteria. If neither can be identified, retain that gap as an open decision instead of treating a diagram update as evidence of agreement.

Provide an understandable explanation of the process and access to the relevant evidence under the organization's arrangements. A reviewer should be able to distinguish the map, an instruction, and a record of an instance of work. The [ISO guidance collection](https://committee.iso.org/home/tc176/iso-9001-auditing-practices-group.html) offers educational papers and expressly states that its guidance is not mandatory audit criteria; applicable requirements still need separate assessment.

A process boundary is an agreement about where the mapped work starts and ends. It is not a claim that work outside the diagram is unimportant. A boundary helps the team identify the inputs it receives, the outputs it hands to another role, and the decisions for which its owner is responsible. Without it, a diagram can expand until no one can maintain it or shrink until the most difficult handoff disappears.

A workflow map is a working explanation of how a selected process proceeds. To make it useful, start with evidence of the work and the people who perform it. The process owner can bring together an operator, a floor supervisor, and the quality lead around a representative record. Their task is to identify the sequence and decisions shown by that example, then note where additional evidence is needed before drawing conclusions.

Traceability is useful when a reviewer can follow a process explanation to the information that supports or guides it and understand the limits of that connection. Select a representative process step, a relevant document, and a completed example where appropriate. The process owner explains the relationship, a worker follows the route, and the quality lead records what was observed and what remains uncertain.
## Define owner responsibilities

The [ICC page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes controlled documents and standard clauses linked to processes. Ask the vendor to demonstrate a process-to-document link using a sample chosen by the plant. Then ask what happens when that document is revised, withdrawn, or temporarily unavailable. The published description is a starting point for the test; it does not establish the behavior of every revision or permission scenario.

The [ICC description](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) presents a top-level process map and detailed flowcharts. Use that description as a point of comparison when designing an overview. It does not establish the layout, navigation, or configuration of a particular installation. Ask for a demonstration of the proposed arrangement using the organization's own sample, and distinguish what is shown from what remains a design question.

The [ICC page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes process flowcharts beneath a top-level map. Treat that as a published description of the vendor's approach, then ask to see how a representative flow could be represented in the proposed configuration. Do not assume particular symbols, editing controls, or automatic behavior unless demonstrated and accepted for the intended use.

The [ICC page](https://isocertificationconsultants.ca/solutions/processes/) describes a top-level map, flowcharts, owners, and links to controlled documents. Use those descriptions to ask how the proposed configuration will represent the organization's selected information. The published page does not establish that every relationship will be transferred automatically. Ask for a demonstration and record which parts require a decision or manual preparation.

The process owner is responsible for agreeing on the purpose with the people who use the process. The inputs are the current work, the records it produces, and the questions the organization needs answered. The owner decides which workflow to examine and records that choice with the map. If the people involved cannot agree on the purpose, record the disagreement and resolve it before treating the map as a basis for a software decision.

The input to the evaluation should include a current map or draft, an example record, and a list of known exceptions. The process owner agrees on what the team will test and who will judge the result. The quality lead records the decision, including evidence observed and questions left open. If there is no agreed process owner, record that gap before treating a demonstration as a reliable indication of operational readiness.

The quality lead can assemble a working list from existing maps and process records. The process owners and operations manager then examine the list together. For each item, identify its purpose, the people who depend on its output, and whether it belongs within the scope of the proposed architecture. Record disputed entries and the person who will resolve them. When two groups claim the same activity, identify the decision that belongs to each before deciding whether the overview needs one entry or two. A list compiled by one department may omit work that another department treats as an essential input.

Start with the agreed process scope and representative records. The quality lead can bring the current map, the accepted overview, and unresolved boundary questions to a meeting with the proposed owner and operations manager. Ask what decisions arise in the process, what information is needed for each, and who must contribute. Record the proposed responsibilities and any disagreement before treating the assignment as complete.
